branches.name: The one church
branches.note: From Pentecost, one communion — spreading from Jerusalem through the whole Mediterranean world, in Greek, Syriac, Latin, Coptic, and Armenian voices.

branches.name: Church of the East
branches.note: After the Council of Ephesus (431) condemned Nestorius, the church of the Persian Empire went its own way — formalized at the Synod of Beth Lapat (484). Its missionaries reached India and Tang-dynasty China centuries before the West did.
branches.includes: Assyrian Church of the East · Ancient Church of the East

branches.name: Oriental Orthodox
branches.note: The churches that could not accept the Council of Chalcedon (451). They confess one united divine-human nature in Christ (miaphysitism) — not the "monophysite" caricature long pinned on them. Armenia's church formally rejected Chalcedon at the councils of Dvin in the 6th century.
branches.includes: Armenian · Coptic · Ethiopian · Eritrean · Syriac · Malankara

branches.name: Eastern Orthodox
branches.note: The Great Schism: centuries of drift over papal authority, the filioque clause, and culture ended with mutual excommunications in 1054 — aimed at individuals, but never healed. The sack of Constantinople by crusaders in 1204 sealed it.
branches.includes: Greek · Russian · Serbian · Romanian · Antiochian and more

branches.name: Catholic
branches.note: The Western church under the bishop of Rome — after 1054, a distinct communion; after 1517, the branch the Reformation left. Today the largest single Christian body.

branches.name: Lutheran
branches.note: Luther's protest against indulgences (1517) became a communion of its own once Rome and the reformers could not be reconciled.

branches.name: Reformed
branches.note: The Swiss reformation of Zwingli and Calvin — Geneva's Institutes date from 1536. Presbyterian and Reformed churches worldwide descend from it.

branches.name: Anglican
branches.note: England's Act of Supremacy (1534) put the crown, not the pope, at the head of the English church — a split born of politics that grew its own theology.
branches.includes: Church of England · the Anglican Communion

branches.name: Anabaptist
branches.note: The radical reformation: believer's baptism, separation from the state — persecuted by Catholics and Protestants alike.

branches.name: Baptist
branches.note: English separatists in Amsterdam (1609) formed the first Baptist congregation; today one of the largest Protestant families.

branches.name: Methodist
branches.note: John Wesley's revival movement inside the Church of England became a church of its own after 1784.

branches.name: Pentecostal
branches.note: The Azusa Street revival (1906) — a one-eyed African-American preacher's mission in Los Angeles — became the fastest-growing Christian stream on earth.
branches.includes: Assemblies of God · countless independent churches
